analysis.one_liner: Caps patient drug copays so they never exceed what the drug actually costs.
analysis.headline: Freshly introduced bill with no cosponsors and no committee action; referred to three House committees two months before the session ends.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar health plans and insurers from charging patients more out of pocket for a prescription drug than the drug's nationwide average retail price at pharmacies. It applies the cap to employer plans, individual insurance, and requires the pharmacy benefit managers working for plans to comply too. The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to three House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: People with health insurance who fill prescriptions, especially those with high copays or coinsurance on expensive drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and insurers from imposing copays, deductibles, or coinsurance on a covered outpatient drug dispensed at an in-network pharmacy above the nationwide average of consumer purchase prices for that drug.
Requires plans and insurers to ensure their pharmacy benefit managers comply with the same cap, closing a common workaround.
Uses an existing Medicaid drug pricing survey to determine the benchmark price.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, self-insured employers, and pharmacy benefit managers, who would collect less in patient cost-sharing; some cost may shift to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Limiting what patients pay without regulating list prices could cause insurers to raise premiums or drug copay benchmarks elsewhere.
No evidence the bill can move: no cosponsors, no committee action, and the session ends in months.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — patients never paying more out of pocket than a drug actually costs — is substantial and directly aimed at a well-known cost-shifting problem. The tradeoff is higher premiums or plan costs. But with no cosponsors and no committee action, it likely won't get a vote.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to three House committees in August 2026; no action since, and the session ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Referred to Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce on the day of introduction.
No hearings, markups, or votes have been recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If it stalls, the status quo prevails: insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep collecting drug cost-sharing above retail price.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; bill awaits committee action

for.name: Rep. Hillary J. Scholten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors and no recorded votes, so the partisan shape is unknown.

industries.note: Would be required to comply with the cost-sharing cap rather than collecting spread above drug price.
Would have to cap patient drug cost-sharing at retail price, reducing collected revenue.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, referral to three committees, and only a few months left in the session, the bill almost certainly dies without a hearing or vote.
